indelible

in-DEL-ih-bul -- Latin in- ('not') + delere ('to destroy, erase'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indelible is impossible to remove, fade, or forget, especially a mark, impression, or memory.

The stain from the spilled ink left an indelible mark on the antique tablecloth.

Example

Decades later, she could still recall every detail of that summer -- an indelible memory that never faded no matter how much time passed.

That kind of mark, impression, or memory that simply refuses to fade or be erased over time is exactly what indelible describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lasting: Lasting simply means continuing for a long time — a lasting friendship, a lasting effect. Indelible is stronger and more specific: an indelible mark or memory cannot be removed or forgotten no matter what is tried. Something lasting endures; something indelible resists every attempt to erase it.

ingrained: Ingrained describes a habit or attitude worked so deep into a person that it operates automatically, built up through years of repetition. Indelible instead describes a mark, impression, or memory that cannot be erased. A routine becomes ingrained slowly; a single vivid moment can be indelible at once.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

temporary: lasting only a short time

erasable: able to be removed or rubbed out

Where it sits · how impossible it is to erase

unforgettable → indelible → permanent

unforgettable vs. indelible: Unforgettable is weaker than indelible: an unforgettable trip stays vivid in memory, while an indelible one is stamped so deep it could never fade even if you tried to erase it.

permanent vs. indelible: Permanent goes further than indelible: an indelible scar resists every attempt to remove it, while a permanent one is fixed forever, with no possibility of change at all.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — -del-: to destroy, erase (Latin (delere))

suffix — -ible: able to be (Latin)

Put it together: Indelible combines in- ('not') with delere ('to destroy, erase') and -ible ('able to be') -- so something indelible is, quite literally, not able to be erased.

Use the root in a new word: delete: She hovered over the delete key for a full minute before closing the laptop instead.

Root Check

Word Choice

Indelible describes a specific mark, impression, or memory that resists fading or erasing -- an indelible stain, an indelible impression, an indelible memory. Contrast this with immutable (taught earlier in this course), which describes a state, law, or fact that cannot change, rather than a sensory mark or memory that simply refuses to fade.
